content.text: On a sunny day, you can feel the warmth of the sun on your face. The sun is 150 million kilometres away, and the space between the sun and the Earth is an almost perfect vacuum. There are no particles to conduct or convect heat across this vast emptiness. So how does the sun's energy reach us? The answer is radiation: specifically, infrared radiation, which is part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Unlike conduction and convection, radiation does not require any material medium to travel through. It can cross the vacuum of space at the speed of light.

In this lesson, we will explore how thermal radiation works, what affects how well objects emit and absorb radiation, and how this knowledge is applied in practical designs from vacuum flasks to buildings. We will also compare all three methods of heat transfer.

Thermal radiation is the transfer of thermal energy by electromagnetic waves, primarily infrared radiation. All objects emit thermal radiation, and the hotter an object is, the more radiation it emits.

All objects at a temperature above absolute zero emit thermal radiation. The amount of radiation emitted depends on:

Hotter objects emit significantly more radiation than cooler objects. The rate of emission increases very rapidly with temperature. In fact, the total energy radiated per unit area is proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature (Stefan-Boltzmann law):

Dark-coloured surfaces emit radiation more effectively than light-coloured surfaces at the same temperature. A matt black surface is the most effective emitter.
Rough (matt) surfaces emit radiation more effectively than smooth (shiny) surfaces. A matt black surface emits more radiation than a shiny black surface.
A larger surface area emits more total radiation. This is why radiators and heat sinks have fins: to increase the surface area available for emission.
Objects also absorb thermal radiation that falls on them. The rate of absorption depends on:
Dark-coloured surfaces absorb radiation more effectively than light-coloured surfaces. A black car parked in the sun gets much hotter inside than a white car.
Rough (matt) surfaces absorb radiation more effectively than smooth (shiny) surfaces. A matt black surface is the best absorber.
A larger surface area absorbs more total radiation.
There is an important symmetry here:
good emitters are also good absorbers, and poor emitters are also poor absorbers
. A matt black surface is both the best emitter and the best absorber of radiation. A shiny silver surface is both a poor emitter and a poor absorber (it is a good reflector instead).
Surfaces that are poor absorbers of radiation are good reflectors. Shiny, light-coloured surfaces reflect most of the radiation that falls on them. This is why:
Emergency blankets (space blankets) are shiny silver: they reflect your body's radiation back toward you, reducing heat loss.
Firefighters' suits have a shiny silver outer layer to reflect the intense radiation from fires.
Buildings in hot climates often have white or light-coloured walls and roofs to reflect solar radiation and stay cooler.
The Leslie's cube is a classic experiment that demonstrates how the surface of an object affects its ability to emit (and absorb) thermal radiation.
A Leslie's cube is a hollow metal cube with four different surfaces:

The cube is filled with hot water, so all four faces are at the same temperature. An infrared detector (such as a thermopile or infrared thermometer) is placed at the same distance from each face in turn, and the intensity of radiation from each face is measured.

| Surface | Relative Radiation Emitted |
|---------|---------------------------|
| Matt black | Highest |
| Matt white | High |
| Shiny black | Moderate |
| Shiny silver | Lowest |
: Dark surfaces emit more radiation than light surfaces (matt black > matt white).
: Matt surfaces emit more radiation than shiny surfaces (matt black > shiny black).
: The matt black surface is the best emitter, and the shiny silver surface is the worst emitter.

The experiment can also be done in reverse: if the cube is placed in a cold environment and the detector measures which surface cools the fastest, the matt black surface cools the most quickly (because it emits radiation the fastest).

A similar experiment with absorption uses the cube at room temperature and directs a heat lamp at each surface. The matt black surface heats up the fastest because it absorbs radiation most effectively.

The spectrum of radiation emitted by a black body depends only on its temperature, not on the material it is made of.
As a black body gets hotter, it emits more radiation at all wavelengths, and the peak of the spectrum shifts to shorter wavelengths.

The vacuum flask (Thermos flask) is an excellent example of a device designed to minimise all three methods of heat transfer. Understanding its design brings together everything we have learned about conduction, convection, and radiation.
Double-walled glass or steel container with a vacuum between the walls:
(no particles to vibrate and pass energy along)
Silvered (shiny) inner surfaces of the walls:
The shiny surface is a poor emitter of radiation, so the hot liquid inside loses little energy by radiation
The shiny surface is also a good reflector, so any radiation emitted by the liquid is reflected back
The shiny surface on the outer wall is a poor absorber, reducing radiation absorbed from the surroundings

The vacuum flask works both ways: it keeps hot drinks hot (by preventing heat from escaping) and cold drinks cold (by preventing heat from entering).
The greenhouse effect is a natural process that warms the Earth's surface, and it involves thermal radiation:
The sun emits short-wavelength radiation (mainly visible light and ultraviolet), which passes through the Earth's atmosphere relatively easily.
This radiation is absorbed by the Earth's surface, warming it.
The warm Earth's surface emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation back toward space.
Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere (such as carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour) absorb some of this outgoing infrared radiation.
These gases then re-emit the infrared radiation in all directions, including back toward the Earth's surface.

This "trapping" of infrared radiation keeps the Earth's surface warmer than it would be without an atmosphere. Without the greenhouse effect, the average surface temperature of the Earth would be about

The enhanced greenhouse effect (global warming) occurs when human activities increase the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, causing more infrared radiation to be absorbed and re-emitted, leading to additional warming.

Worked Example 1: Understanding Emission and Absorption

Two identical metal cans are placed side by side. Can A is painted matt black and Can B is painted shiny silver. Both are filled with hot water at the same temperature. Which can will cool faster? Explain using the concept of thermal radiation.

Can A (matt black) will cool faster. The matt black surface is a much better emitter of infrared radiation than the shiny silver surface. At the same temperature, the matt black can radiates energy to its surroundings at a much higher rate. Therefore, the water in Can A loses thermal energy faster and its temperature drops more quickly.
Can B (shiny silver) is a poor emitter of radiation. Its shiny surface reflects much of the radiation back rather than emitting it. The water in Can B retains its heat for longer.
This can be verified experimentally by measuring the water temperature in each can at regular intervals. The temperature of the water in the matt black can decreases faster.
A solar water heater has a matt black collector panel facing the sun. Explain why the panel is painted matt black rather than white or silver.

The matt black surface is chosen because it is the best absorber of thermal radiation. When solar radiation (including infrared and visible light) strikes the matt black panel, almost all of it is absorbed and converted to thermal energy, which heats the water flowing through the panel.
A white surface would reflect most of the solar radiation, absorbing very little. A silver surface would reflect even more. Neither would be effective at absorbing solar energy to heat the water.
The matt texture is also important because matt surfaces absorb better than shiny surfaces. A shiny black surface would absorb less radiation than a matt black surface.

Despite all these measures, the flask is not perfect. Some heat is still lost through conduction along the glass walls themselves, through the stopper, and through the supports. This is why a hot drink in a vacuum flask will eventually cool down, but much more slowly than in an ordinary cup.
Explain why the temperature inside a car parked in the sun becomes much higher than the outside temperature.
This is an example of the greenhouse effect in a small-scale system:
Short-wavelength solar radiation (visible light) passes easily through the car's glass windows.
This radiation is absorbed by the surfaces inside the car (seats, dashboard, steering wheel), warming them up.
The warm surfaces inside the car emit longer-wavelength infrared radiation.
Glass is largely opaque to (does not transmit) long-wavelength infrared radiation. The infrared radiation cannot pass back out through the windows.
The infrared radiation is trapped inside the car, and the air inside heats up through convection from the hot surfaces.

Since the energy coming in (through the transparent glass) exceeds the energy getting out (infrared is blocked by the glass), the temperature inside continues to rise until a new equilibrium is reached, at a temperature significantly higher than the outside.
This is similar to how greenhouse gases in the atmosphere allow short-wavelength solar radiation in but absorb outgoing long-wavelength infrared radiation.

All objects above absolute zero emit thermal radiation. A cold object emits less radiation than a hot object, but it still emits some. Even an ice cube emits infrared radiation, just less than the warmer objects around it.

A black surface is a better absorber of radiation, so it heats up faster when radiation falls on it. But a black surface is also a better emitter, so it cools down faster when there is no radiation source. Whether a black object is hotter depends on the situation.
Misconception 3: "Radiation only travels in straight lines from a source"
Radiation is emitted in all directions from any surface. It does travel in straight lines (it is an electromagnetic wave), but it is emitted from every point on a surface in all directions.
Misconception 4: "A vacuum flask keeps hot things hot and cannot keep cold things cold"

A vacuum flask works both ways. It minimises heat transfer in both directions. A cold drink stays cold because heat from the outside environment is prevented from reaching the drink, using the same mechanisms that prevent heat from escaping a hot drink.
Misconception 5: "Thermal radiation is the same as radioactivity"

Thermal radiation (infrared radiation) is electromagnetic radiation and is completely safe at normal levels. Radioactivity involves the emission of particles (alpha, beta) or very high-energy electromagnetic waves (gamma rays) from unstable atomic nuclei. These are entirely different phenomena.
Misconception 6: "White surfaces are the best reflectors of thermal radiation"

Actually, shiny metallic (silver) surfaces are the best reflectors of infrared radiation. White surfaces reflect visible light well but are not as effective at reflecting infrared radiation as polished metal surfaces.
Misconception 7: "The greenhouse effect is entirely harmful"
The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life on Earth. Without it, the Earth's average temperature would be about
, making the planet largely uninhabitable. It is the enhanced greenhouse effect (the additional warming caused by human-produced greenhouse gases) that causes concern.
